verdicts.quote: The method reads a 32-bit unsigned integer from the network and uses it to allocate a byte array. The code `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` allows allocation of up to Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 bytes (approximately 2 GB). An attacker sending a frame with contentLength near 2 GB will exhaust available heap memory, causing OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.
verdicts.why: F01 is about exactly the mechanism in D1: an attacker-controlled length field (contentLength) taken straight off the wire sizes the byte[] allocation, and the array is allocated on the strength of that number alone - the only check is an upper bound against Integer.MAX_VALUE, never that the frame actually carries that many payload bytes. That is what F01 says is exploitable (a small frame declaring ~2 GB exhausts the heap), not something it mentions in passing.

No finding is about mutually recursive decoding with no depth counter. The list has only two items: F01 (unbounded allocation from a length field) and F02. The closest is F02, but it is about a different mechanism entirely - arithmetic overflow of `in.readLong()*1000` in timestamp conversion producing a negative Date - which concerns a single scalar value, not nested/self-referential input driving recursion depth. Nothing in either finding mentions recursion, nesting, call depth, or stack exhaustion.
